lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Giovanna Waltrick | Lesson 2 -- My Life, My Story

listenings.text: People ask me what I actually do all day, and the honest answer is that I have the same conversation about four hundred times. I look at a passport, I look at the person in front of me, and I ask three or four questions. Each conversation takes less than a minute. There are only three things I really need to hear. Why you are here. How long you are staying. And where you are staying while you are in the country. That is it. Almost everybody in that line is nervous, and I want to say this clearly: being nervous is not a problem for me. I see it four hundred times a day. What I need is a clear answer, not a confident one. Short is fine. And if you did not understand my question, ask me to repeat it. I would much rather repeat a question than hear the answer to a different one.

The first time I went through passport control without my parents, I gave myself a job in the line. Instead of standing there imagining everything that could go wrong, I practised my answers in my head, and I wrote three words on my phone: tourism, two weeks, and the name of the hotel. That was all. When my turn came, I answered the first question, I answered the second one, and then I did not understand the third one at all. I heard the words but nothing arrived. So I said, sorry, could you repeat that, please. And he repeated it, more slowly, and I answered it. Nothing happened. Nobody wrote anything down. I think that is the part nobody tells you: asking somebody to repeat a question is completely normal, and it is much better than guessing and answering the wrong thing.
